The reproductive biology of White steenbras (Lithognathus lithognathus) remains relatively poorly documented, though available data from congeneric sparids provide useful benchmarks. Based on comparative work with Diplodus puntazzo, the larval phase is brief, with yolk-sac absorption and the onset of exogenous feeding occurring just 6.5 days [ab = 6.5 days] after fertilization when eggs are incubated at a stable temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This rapid developmental pace is typical of temperate sparids that spawn during the austral spring, when water temperatures begin to rise and planktonic food resources become abundant. The fertilised ova are themselves minute; extrapolations from the egg diameter of the closely related Diplodus sargus yield an estimated wet weight at birth of only 0.00032 g [Wwb = 0.00032 g], a value that underscores the extreme energetic vulnerability of the newly emerged yolk-sac larva. This tiny initial mass imposes a narrow window for successful first feeding before the endogenous yolk reserves are exhausted, a constraint that likely exerts strong selective pressure on spawning site selection and the timing of gamete release in this species.

As juveniles recruit to estuarine and nearshore habitats, Lithognathus lithognathus undergoes a prolonged growth phase that culminates in a remarkably large adult body size. The ultimate total length attained by this species appears to be approximately 110 cm [Li = approximately 110 cm], a figure that, while lower than the 200 cm sometimes cited in older compilations, aligns more consistently with the length-frequency distributions observed in modern fishery-independent surveys. Corresponding to this asymptotic length, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is estimated at roughly 25,000 g [Wwi = roughly 25,000 g], derived from length-weight relationships parameterised for the species. This places White steenbras among the larger members of the Sparidae, with individuals requiring many years of sustained somatic growth to approach such dimensions. The ecological implications are significant: large body size confers refuge from most piscine predators and allows adults to exploit a broader range of benthic prey, including hard-shelled molluscs and decapod crustaceans that smaller conspecifics cannot handle.

The transition to reproductive maturity occurs well before maximum size is attained. Field studies indicate that the total length at which 50% of individuals are sexually mature is approximately 54 cm [Lp = approximately 54 cm], a length that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of roughly 2861 g [Wwp = roughly 2861 g]. This size threshold likely reflects the point at which sufficient body cavity volume exists to accommodate the developing gonads, as well as the accumulation of adequate energy reserves to support the metabolic demands of gametogenesis. In the context of the species' overall life history, maturation at just under half the ultimate length suggests a strategy that balances the benefits of early reproduction against the continued advantages of somatic growth; postponing maturity further would allow larger clutch sizes but would also increase the risk of mortality before any offspring are produced. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) was a typical value of 5% [GSI = 5%], recorded for actively spawning females held under controlled conditions at 16 °C [T = 16 °C].

Longevity in White steenbras is considerable, consistent with its large body size and iteroparous reproductive schedule. The oldest individuals on record have been estimated to live for approximately 22 years [am = approximately 22 years] at a typical thermal regime of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], a lifespan that reflects a relatively slow pace of life typical of late-maturing, large-bodied sparids in subtropical and warm-temperate waters. Such extended lifespans allow multiple annual spawning events over several decades, a reproductive strategy that buffers populations against years of poor recruitment. The trade-off is a delayed onset of reproduction relative to shorter-lived species, a feature that makes populations of L. lithognathus particularly sensitive to overexploitation of larger, older individuals.

Comparative life-history data from related sparids offer additional context for interpreting the measurements reported for White steenbras. The estimated lifespan of 22 years [am = 22 years] is broadly consistent with values documented for other large members of the genus, many of which exhibit maximum ages between 15 and 30 years in unexploited populations at a temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. The total length at puberty of 54 cm [Lp = 54 cm] and its corresponding wet weight of 2861 g [Wwp = 2861 g] align closely with the maturation schedules of other lithognathid species from similar latitudes, though intraspecific variation attributable to local environmental conditions and fishing pressure has been noted in some coastal regions. The ultimate wet weight of 25,000 g [Wwi = 25,000 g] that accompanies an asymptotic length of 110 cm [Li = 110 cm] is consistent with the deep-bodied, robust morphology characteristic of adult White steenbras, contrasting with the more fusiform shapes of faster-growing congeners. The minute wet weight at birth of 0.00032 g [Wwb = 0.00032 g] and the short age at birth of 6.5 days [ab = 6.5 days] at 16 °C [T = 16 °C] are typical of pelagic-spawning sparids, whose small eggs and rapid embryonic development are adaptations to a planktonic larval phase. The gonadosomatic index of 5% [GSI = 5%] was recorded at 16 °C [T = 16 °C].
